screens.title: Debugging and Error Handling in Unity
screens.narratorSegment: Debugging is an essential skill that turns confusion into clarity. In this chapter you will learn three practical ways to locate and fix runtime problems in Unity: clear Console logging, stepping through code with a debugger, and structured error handling with try-catch. We’ll show how to use log levels to surface relevant information, attach Visual Studio to pause and inspect state at a breakpoint, and write defensive checks to avoid the common NullReferenceException. You will also practice a simple hands-on activity that replicates a missing reference bug and then fix it using a defensive Awake check and an informative error log. These techniques reduce time spent guessing and help you ship stable gameplay logic. By the end, you’ll be able to read the call stack, choose when to use try-catch for external operations, and prevent frequent Unity runtime failures with small code checks. Think of this chapter as building a developer habit: log with context, pause and inspect, then harden code where necessary. Which of these three steps do you expect will save you the most time in your next playtest?

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Part 1
screens.narratorSegment: These learning objectives map to practical debugging skills you’ll use every day. First, you will learn to use Unity’s Console effectively: not just to print data, but to craft messages that immediately reveal where and why something happened. That skill reduces the time spent scanning logs during a playtest. Second, you will integrate Visual Studio’s debugger with Unity to set breakpoints and inspect variables. Pausing execution and watching variable changes is the fastest way to confirm assumptions about state and sequence. Third, you will implement try-catch blocks to handle external failures, like missing save files or failed network calls, so errors don’t crash gameplay. Finally, you’ll learn to identify and fix a NullReferenceException — one of the most common runtime errors — by diagnosing why a reference is null and how to respond. Each card below explains the competency and gives a short visual mnemonic to help you remember when to use it. These are practical habits that make your development cycles faster and less frustrating.

screens.title: Unity Console and Log Levels
screens.narratorSegment: The Unity Console is the first place to look when something behaves unexpectedly. A log entry is a structured signal: an informational log communicates normal runtime data, a warning indicates a suspicious but non-fatal condition, and an error signals a critical problem that often halts normal behavior in the editor. Use informational logs for confirmed state values such as positions or scores. Use warnings for recoverable but surprising states — for example, when an optional asset is missing and you plan a fallback. Use errors when a required condition is broken, like a missing weapon prefab before instantiation. A concrete example: log the player name and health as context, not just the word "health". Instead of printing a bare number, include the object identity and the variable name so the message is actionable during team debugging. A common misconception is that more logs are always better; noisy, context-free logs make the Console unusable. Prefer fewer, richer messages and use levels to filter. Key takeaway: well-formed logs are your first defense — they make it fast to reproduce problems and decide whether to step into the debugger or apply a code fix. Ask yourself: what three pieces of context would let someone understand this log without opening the code?

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › Unity Console
Definition

Log levels and purpose

Informational logs report normal state, warnings flag suspicious but recoverable situations, and errors indicate failures requiring attention. Use each level intentionally so filters help you focus.

Debug.Log • Info
Print values and state during gameplay to confirm expected behavior.
Debug.LogWarning • Warning
Highlight unexpected but non-fatal conditions you may want to handle later.
Debug.LogError • Error
Report critical issues such as required asset missing or logic that must not run.
Practical Example
// Example: include context in logs
Debug.Log("Spawned Player: " + player.name + " at " + transform.position);
Debug.LogWarning("Missing sprite for enemy type: " + enemyType);
Debug.LogError("Weapon Prefab not assigned on " + gameObject.name);
Common mistake
Printing values without context creates ambiguous logs that waste time during debugging.
Key Takeaway

Choose log level deliberately and always include who/what/where to make messages actionable.

screens.title: Crafting Useful Log Messages
screens.narratorSegment: A short process improves every log you write. First, identify the intent: are you confirming a state, warning of a fallback, or signaling a failure? Second, include context: object name, relevant variables, and a descriptive label. Third, include a small payload: only the values you need to diagnose the issue. Fourth, choose the correct log level so you can filter messages during playtests. For example, when spawning an enemy, a good log might include the enemy type, spawn position, and the method that requested the spawn. A common misconception is thinking more data equals better logs. Extra data increases noise and slows diagnosis. Instead, prefer concise, structured messages that answer who, what, and why. Practice: pick a noisy scene in your project and rewrite three frequent logs using this process. You will notice fewer repeated entries and faster problem isolation. Closing question: which two fields would you add to a spawn log to make reproduction immediate? Crafting Useful Log Messages means decide intent, add context, include minimal payload, and pick the right level to keep logs actionable.. In practical terms, a simple process to make every log entry immediately actionable.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › Crafting Logs
Process

Four-step recipe for useful logs

1
Intent
Decide if the log confirms state, warns, or reports an error.
2
Context
Include object name, method, or other identifiers so the message locates itself.
3
Payload
Attach only the values needed to diagnose the issue.
4
Level
Choose Info, Warning, or Error so filters expose the right entries during play.
Example
// Spawn log example
Debug.Log("SpawnEnemy | type=" + enemyType + " | spawnerId=" + spawnerId + " | pos=" + spawnPoint);
Key Takeaway

A clear, contextual log saves minutes of investigation during a playtest.

Check your understanding
Rewrite one noisy log from your project following this recipe and compare how fast you find a bug.

screens.title: Attach Visual Studio Debugger
screens.narratorSegment: Attaching Visual Studio to the Unity editor gives you a live window into your program’s execution. Begin by ensuring Visual Studio Tools for Unity is installed. Then, in Visual Studio use the Attach Unity Debugger option and select the running Unity instance. Once attached, set breakpoints by clicking the left margin next to a line of C# code. When Unity reaches that line, execution will pause and Visual Studio highlights the current instruction. Pausing allows you to examine local variables, object properties, and the call stack. You can inspect the Locals window to see current variable values and use Watch to pin important expressions. Step Over moves to the next line, Step Into jumps into a called method, and Continue resumes normal execution. A concrete example: set a breakpoint right before a weapon instantiation to confirm whether the prefab reference is null. A common misunderstanding is that breakpoints alter program timing in a way that creates different behavior; while pausing can affect timing, it reveals state that would otherwise be ephemeral and is indispensable for understanding hard-to-reproduce issues. End by asking: which variable in your next bug would you watch as you step through?

keyIdea.title: Why use a debugger
keyIdea.text: A debugger reveals runtime state and the sequence of execution so you can confirm assumptions and find logic errors quickly.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › Attach Debugger
Quick Architecture
Attach VS → set breakpoints → run Unity → pause and inspect.
Attach
In Visual Studio choose Attach Unity Debugger and select the Unity editor instance.
Breakpoint
Click the left margin in a C# file to set a breakpoint on a line you want to inspect.
Inspect
Use Locals, Watch, and Call Stack windows to see current values and the execution path.
Example Walkthrough
Set a breakpoint on the line that instantiates a weapon prefab. Run the scene and let the breakpoint pause execution. Hover over the prefab variable or check Locals to confirm whether it is null. If it is null, the inspector assignment was missed or the prefab reference was not set up by your spawning logic.
Common misconception
Pausing execution changes timing and may hide race conditions. Use it to inspect state, then craft tests to reproduce without pausing.
Key Takeaway

Use the debugger to observe real runtime state and confirm or refute assumptions quickly.

screens.title: Breakpoints, Stepping, and Inspecting
screens.narratorSegment: Breakpoints let you stop execution at a precise line and observe program state right before a critical operation. In C# scripts used in Unity, pick a line with a suspected side effect — for example, an Instantiate call or a call that modifies a shared field — and set a breakpoint there. When execution pauses, inspect Locals to see current values and the Call Stack to find the exact chain of calls that led to this point. Use Step Over to run the current line without entering called methods, and Step Into to dive into a method's internals when you need to inspect nested logic. A concrete example: set a breakpoint on the line where _currentWeapon. transform. parent = transform is called. If _currentWeapon is null the debugger will show it in Locals and you will quickly see the null. A common misconception is that stepping fixes the problem; it only reveals the state. After you identify the null, apply a defensive check or fix the assignment path. Closing question: which breakpoint would you set to verify a variable changes after a method returns?

keyIdea.title: Stepping tip
keyIdea.text: Set breakpoints on suspected lines and step into functions to see how values change across calls.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › Breakpoints & Stepping
Code Example
void Start()
{
  _currentWeapon = Instantiate(weaponPrefab, transform.position, Quaternion.identity);
  // Breakpoint candidate: next line
  _currentWeapon.transform.parent = transform;
}
Place a breakpoint on the commented line. When paused, hover or check the Locals window to see whether _currentWeapon is null and inspect weaponPrefab and transform values.
Inspection Tools
  • Locals: shows local variables and their current values.
  • Watch: pin expressions you care about across breakpoints.
  • Call Stack: follow the order of method calls to trace origins.
Key Takeaway

Use breakpoints to capture transient state and step to confirm how values evolve during execution.

screens.title: NullReferenceException — Causes and Detection
screens.narratorSegment: A NullReferenceException occurs when code attempts to use a reference variable that points to nothing. In Unity this commonly happens when an Inspector field is left unassigned, when GetComponent returns null because the component is absent, or when FindObjectOfType fails to find a matching object. The exception tells you the line where the access happened and the call stack leading to it. Use the Console entry to jump to the script line and then attach a debugger or add a targeted log to examine why the reference is null. For example, a common scenario is a public GameObject field left empty in the Inspector; trying to call SetActive on that field will generate an NRE. A key misconception is assuming NREs are caused by value types or by the transform being null — in Unity, transform on a valid GameObject is never null. Always check the reference itself first. Concrete detection steps: read the Console line and call stack, inspect the variable at that line in the debugger, and then trace upstream to where the reference should have been assigned. Takeaway: locating the first null in the chain often solves the error and stops downstream failures.

keyIdea.title: NRE root cause
keyIdea.text: An NRE means a reference was null; check the reference, not the property you tried to access, and trace where it should have been set.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › NullReferenceException
What it means

A reference variable points to nothing and code attempts to access a member on it.

Common causes
  • Inspector field left unassigned.
  • GetComponent returned null because component is missing.
  • FindObjectOfType did not find a matching object.
Detection steps
  1. Open Console and read the exception line.
  2. Inspect the variable at that line in the debugger or add a targeted log.
  3. Trace where the reference should have been assigned and validate that path.
Example
Attempting _playerRigidbody.velocity when _playerRigidbody is null causes an NRE. Check the reference in Awake or disable the script and log an error so the game won’t crash later.
Common misconception
Assuming transform can be null. If the GameObject exists, transform is valid. Check the reference variable itself first.
Key Takeaway

Find the first null in the assignment chain and fix or guard that assignment to stop the NRE.

screens.title: Defensive Programming Patterns
screens.narratorSegment: Defensive programming reduces the number of runtime surprises by validating assumptions early. A common Unity pattern is to perform critical checks in Awake: attempt to resolve missing components, and if a required reference is still null, log an error and disable the script to prevent further exceptions. The Awake example in this chapter shows retrieving a Rigidbody with GetComponent and then checking for null. If missing, the code logs an error referencing the GameObject name and sets enabled to false to stop Update from running. This is a small, visible action that prevents cascades of NullReferenceExceptions later. Another pattern is to guard every use-site with a null check when a reference might be legitimately absent under certain conditions. Use try-catch blocks only around external, exceptional operations like file input and output or network calls, not to mask logic errors. A misconception is to overuse try-catch as a shortcut for poor validation. Instead, validate inputs and only catch truly exceptional cases. Final question: which checks would you add to an AI spawning routine to avoid null references? Defensive Programming Patterns means validate and fail fast: check required components early and disable unsafe execution paths to avoid cascading errors.. In practical terms, simple checks and fail-fast behavior to prevent runtime exceptions.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Defensive habit

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › Defensive Programming
Pattern

Awake checks and fail-fast

// Defensive programming example
void Awake()
{
  _playerRigidbody = GetComponent<Rigidbody>();
  if (_playerRigidbody == null)
  {
    Debug.LogError("PlayerController requires a Rigidbody on " + gameObject.name, this);
    enabled = false; // stop further execution
    return;
  }
}
Guidelines
  • Check required components early in Awake or Start.
  • Log errors with the object name to make messages actionable.
  • Disable scripts that cannot function to prevent downstream exceptions.
Key Takeaway

Small checks prevent large failure cascades. Prefer validation over catching bugs later.

screens.title: try-catch and finally in C#
screens.narratorSegment: C# try-catch-finally is a structured way to handle operations that may fail at runtime, especially when interacting with external resources like files or networks. Wrap the risky operation inside a try block; if an expected exception occurs, a matching catch block handles it and prevents the program from crashing. Use specific exception types when possible, for example FileNotFoundException, and provide an informative error log and fallback action. The finally block always executes whether an exception happened or not, making it suitable for cleanup tasks like closing file streams. The chapter’s LoadGameData example demonstrates checking file existence, reading contents inside a try, and catching both file-not-found and general exceptions with different handling. Avoid using try-catch to hide logic errors or as a substitute for validation. A common misconception is that try-catch is free and should be used everywhere. It has performance cost and can obscure programming errors if overused. Use it when interacting with input and output, parsing external data, or other operations where external conditions are truly exceptional and uncontrollable. Final reflection: when reading an exception, which specific catch would you add to handle corrupted data gracefully?

It has performance cost and can obscure programming errors if overused. Use it when interacting with input and output, parsing external data, or other operations where external conditions are truly exceptional and uncontrollable. Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › try-catch-finally
LoadGameData Example
public void LoadGameData(string path)
{
  try
  {
    if (!System.IO.File.Exists(path))
      throw new System.IO.FileNotFoundException("Data file not found at " + path);

    string data = System.IO.File.ReadAllText(path);
    Debug.Log("Game data loaded: " + data);
  }
  catch (System.IO.FileNotFoundException ex)
  {
    Debug.LogError("Failed to load game data: " + ex.Message);
  }
  catch (System.Exception ex)
  {
    Debug.LogError("An unexpected error occurred: " + ex.Message);
  }
  finally
  {
    Debug.Log("Attempted to load game data from: " + path);
  }
}
Guidelines
  • Prefer specific catch blocks for expected failures and a general catch for unexpected cases.
  • Use finally to close resources or log attempt completion.
  • Do not use try-catch to mask logic errors; validate inputs first.
Key Takeaway

Try-catch is for external, exceptional problems; validate what you can and catch what you must.

screens.narratorSegment: Beyond NullReferenceException, Unity and C# projects often encounter a small set of recurring exceptions. IndexOutOfRangeException happens when code tries to access an array or list element using an invalid index. ArgumentOutOfRangeException results from passing an invalid argument, for example when min is greater than max in a clamp call. The call stack in the Console helps here by pointing to the line that triggered the exception and the sequence of calls. A misconception is treating these exceptions the same: each has a distinct root cause and a targeted fix. Takeaway: learn the error names and match each to a focused remediation rather than applying a one-size-fits-all approach. fullNarratorScript:
Debugging is an essential skill that turns confusion into clarity. In this chapter you will learn three practical ways to locate and fix runtime problems in Unity: clear Console logging, stepping through code with a debugger, and structured error handling with try-catch. We’ll show how to use log levels to surface relevant information, attach Visual Studio to pause and inspect state at a breakpoint, and write defensive checks to avoid the common NullReferenceException. You will also practice a simple hands-on activity that replicates a missing reference bug and then fix it using a defensive Awake check and an informative error log. These techniques reduce time spent guessing and help you ship stable gameplay logic. By the end, you’ll be able to read the call stack, choose when to use try-catch for external operations, and prevent frequent Unity runtime failures with small code checks. Think of this chapter as building a developer habit: log with context, pause and inspect, then harden code where necessary. Which of these three steps do you expect will save you the most time in your next playtest?

These learning objectives map to practical debugging skills you’ll use every day. First, you will learn to use Unity’s Console effectively: not just to print data, but to craft messages that immediately reveal where and why something happened. That skill reduces the time spent scanning logs during a playtest. Second, you will integrate Visual Studio’s debugger with Unity to set breakpoints and inspect variables. Pausing execution and watching variable changes is the fastest way to confirm assumptions about state and sequence. Third, you will implement try-catch blocks to handle external failures, like missing save files or failed network calls, so errors don’t crash gameplay. Finally, you’ll learn to identify and fix a NullReferenceException — one of the most common runtime errors — by diagnosing why a reference is null and how to respond. Each card below explains the competency and gives a short visual mnemonic to help you remember when to use it. These are practical habits that make your development cycles faster and less frustrating.

This second set of objectives focuses on habits and supporting skills that complement the core debugging tools. You will learn defensive programming techniques so your code proactively checks assumptions before they cause exceptions. You will practice writing log messages with enough context — like object names and key values — so a single log line tells a clear story. You will learn to read the call stack provided by the Console to trace where an exception originated and why it bubbled up. Lastly, you will practice the workflow of reproducing a bug, pausing in the debugger to inspect state, applying a small defensive change, and re-testing. Together, these objectives shape a routine: log with context, reproduce reliably, step and inspect, then harden the code where needed. These habits scale well across teams because they create reproducible signals and prevent intermittent runtime failures from eating development time.

The Unity Console is the first place to look when something behaves unexpectedly. A log entry is a structured signal: an informational log communicates normal runtime data, a warning indicates a suspicious but non-fatal condition, and an error signals a critical problem that often halts normal behavior in the editor. Use informational logs for confirmed state values such as positions or scores. Use warnings for recoverable but surprising states — for example, when an optional asset is missing and you plan a fallback. Use errors when a required condition is broken, like a missing weapon prefab before instantiation. A concrete example: log the player name and health as context, not just the word "health". Instead of printing a bare number, include the object identity and the variable name so the message is actionable during team debugging. A common misconception is that more logs are always better; noisy, context-free logs make the Console unusable. Prefer fewer, richer messages and use levels to filter. Key takeaway: well-formed logs are your first defense — they make it fast to reproduce problems and decide whether to step into the debugger or apply a code fix. Ask yourself: what three pieces of context would let someone understand this log without opening the code?

A short process improves every log you write. First, identify the intent: are you confirming a state, warning of a fallback, or signaling a failure? Second, include context: object name, relevant variables, and a descriptive label. Third, include a small payload: only the values you need to diagnose the issue. Fourth, choose the correct log level so you can filter messages during playtests. For example, when spawning an enemy, a good log might include the enemy type, spawn position, and the method that requested the spawn. A common misconception is thinking more data equals better logs. Extra data increases noise and slows diagnosis. Instead, prefer concise, structured messages that answer who, what, and why. Practice: pick a noisy scene in your project and rewrite three frequent logs using this process. You will notice fewer repeated entries and faster problem isolation. Closing question: which two fields would you add to a spawn log to make reproduction immediate? Crafting Useful Log Messages means decide intent, add context, include minimal payload, and pick the right level to keep logs actionable.. In practical terms, a simple process to make every log entry immediately actionable.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Attaching Visual Studio to the Unity editor gives you a live window into your program’s execution. Begin by ensuring Visual Studio Tools for Unity is installed. Then, in Visual Studio use the Attach Unity Debugger option and select the running Unity instance. Once attached, set breakpoints by clicking the left margin next to a line of C# code. When Unity reaches that line, execution will pause and Visual Studio highlights the current instruction. Pausing allows you to examine local variables, object properties, and the call stack. You can inspect the Locals window to see current variable values and use Watch to pin important expressions. Step Over moves to the next line, Step Into jumps into a called method, and Continue resumes normal execution. A concrete example: set a breakpoint right before a weapon instantiation to confirm whether the prefab reference is null. A common misunderstanding is that breakpoints alter program timing in a way that creates different behavior; while pausing can affect timing, it reveals state that would otherwise be ephemeral and is indispensable for understanding hard-to-reproduce issues. End by asking: which variable in your next bug would you watch as you step through?

Breakpoints let you stop execution at a precise line and observe program state right before a critical operation. In C# scripts used in Unity, pick a line with a suspected side effect — for example, an Instantiate call or a call that modifies a shared field — and set a breakpoint there. A NullReferenceException occurs when code attempts to use a reference variable that points to nothing.
